entities.name: The Great Sphinx
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Great Sphinx of Giza, a colossal limestone statue with the body of a lion and the head of a pharaoh, stands as a monumental emblem of ancient Egypt, created circa 2559 BCE during the reign of Pharaoh Khufu, also known as Cheops. Located on the Giza Plateau, near Cairo, this iconic structure represents not only the architectural prowess of the Fourth Dynasty but also the complexities of ancient Egyptian religious beliefs. The Sphinx, which measures approximately 73 meters long and 20 meters high, has intrigued historians and archaeologists for centuries, serving as a symbol of mystery and national pride for Egypt.

Constructed as part of the extensive funerary complex for Khufu, the Great Sphinx was designed to guard the pyramids, embodying the pharaoh's power and divine connection to the gods. Over the millennia, it has undergone numerous restorations, particularly during the reign of Pharaoh Thutmose IV in the 15th century BCE, who inscribed a dream stela between its paws, detailing a vision in which the Sphinx promised him kingship if he restored it. This act not only highlights the Sphinx's significance in ancient Egyptian culture but also cements its role as a national symbol through subsequent dynasties.

The Sphinx's legacy extends beyond its physical presence; it has influenced art, literature, and popular culture across millennia. As one of the largest and oldest statues in the world, it has inspired countless interpretations, from ancient texts to modern films, and has become a focal point for tourism and archaeological study. Its iconic status is reflected in its depiction in various media, leading to the phrase, 'The Sphinx never tells,' which underscores its enigmatic nature. The Great Sphinx continues to capture the imagination of scholars and visitors alike, representing a bridge between ancient civilizations and contemporary society.
